title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E420 (Novi Commentarii 16, 1771/72) reinterprets the calculus of variations through an auxiliary parameter t. A one-parameter family of curves y(x,t) is introduced, and the variation is the partial differential in t. Sections 32–34 set up the question: given a curve AM and a functional W = ∫Z dx (for example the brachistochrone time ∫√(1+p²)/√x dx), how much does W change when AM is replaced by an infinitely near curve αμ?

This page has three parts.

§34 (end). The integral must be fixed by a lower limit. Normally the starting point A is taken as the origin of integration, so that W(0)=0, or some other given initial abscissa is used. W is then a function of the upper abscissa AP=x.

§35. Admissible comparison curves αμ must be drawn 'with a continuous stroke', with no angles or jumps. In modern terms the varied curves must be at least C¹: no jumps in y and no corners, i.e. no jumps in p=dy/dx. Apart from this they may be 'continuous' in Euler's technical sense (given by a single equation or analytic law) or 'discontinuous' (not given by one analytic law, as if drawn freehand). This is Euler's vibrating-string notion of arbitrary functions, carried into the calculus of variations.

§36 (continued on p.57). A concrete construction of such curves:
- Draw an arbitrary curve BN over the same axis.
- At each abscissa X, take the segment YV between the given curve (point Y) and BN (point V).
- Cut each YV at v in the ratio of finite to infinitely small, so that Yv is an infinitesimal part of YV.
- In modern form: y_t(x) = y(x) + t·(η(x) − y(x)) = y(x) + t·h(x), with h = η − y arbitrary and t infinitesimal.

On p.57 Euler adds that BN must nowhere have a tangent normal to the axis, i.e. h' must be bounded. Then not only are the gaps Yv infinitesimal, but the tangents at Y and v are infinitely nearly parallel. The comparison curves are therefore close in both y and y'. This is precisely a weak (C¹) neighbourhood, and the variation is δy = dt·(∂y/∂t) = Yv.

The construction serves the next section (§37). There the first part of the variation, ∫(∂y/∂t)dt·(N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − …)dx, is read as a sum of local contributions Yv times the Euler–Lagrange expression.
errors: Euler's exclusion of corners is stronger than his construction strictly needs. A corner in BN would give the varied curve only an infinitesimal corner, ε·[η'], and the change in p would still be infinitesimal. His requirement that BN have no vertical tangent (p.57) is the operative one, since it keeps the change in p uniformly infinitesimal.
The varied curve starts at α, not A, unless BN passes through A. Endpoint variations are therefore implicitly allowed, and these are treated later in the paper through the boundary terms.

ideas.what: Integral fixed by a prescribed lower limit (vanishing at the initial point A), making W a function of the upper abscissa.
ideas.modern_name: definite integral as a function of its upper limit

ideas.what: Admissible comparison curves must have no jumps and no corners, but may be 'discontinuous' (not given by a single analytic law, drawn freehand).
ideas.modern_name: admissible class of C¹ (piecewise-arbitrary) variations; Euler's arbitrary functions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (vibrating string debate, 1748 onward); rigorous admissible classes from Weierstrass/du Bois-Reymond
ideas.where_published: Euler's vibrating-string papers (e.g. E119, E213) for discontinuous functions; this paper E420 for the variational application

ideas.what: Construction of the varied curve as y + t(η − y) with η arbitrary and t infinitesimal; requiring no vertical tangent of η ensures the slopes are also infinitely close.
ideas.modern_name: one-parameter variation y + εh; weak variations / weak (C¹) neighbourhood
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange's δ-method (1760) for the variation concept; Euler E420 for the parameter-t form; Weierstrass (1879 lectures) for the explicit weak/strong distinction
ideas.where_published: E420 itself (also E385/E386 use the related t-parameter); discussed by Goldstine (A History of the Calculus of Variations, 1980) and C. Fraser on Euler's variational calculus

missed.claim: Euler explicitly requires comparison curves to be close in slope as well as in position (tangents infinitely nearly parallel), i.e. a weak neighbourhood, while also admitting non-analytic ('discontinuous') comparison functions. This is an early explicit statement of the admissible class for the first variation. However, historians of the calculus of variations (Goldstine, Fraser) discuss E420's parameter interpretation, so this is likely already noted, if under-emphasised.
missed.quote: has curuas continuo quodam tractu ductas esse debere, ita vt in iis nusquam anguli aliiue saltus deprehendantur; ... siue sint adeo discontinuae, quasi libero manus motu ductae
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It shows a conscious weak-variation hypothesis about a century before Weierstrass's weak/strong distinction. It also shows Euler's 'discontinuous functions' from the string debate being imported into variational calculus; this is mostly of historiographical interest.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is foundational and nicely explicit: it gives a C¹/weak-neighbourhood requirement and admits arbitrary 'discontinuous' comparison functions. But E420 and its geometric interpretation of variations are known and discussed in the standard histories, and no new result appears here.
transcription_corrections: Long-s rendered as 'f' throughout: 'euanefcat', 'pofito', 'ftatui', 'abfciffae', 'refpondebit', 'faltus', 'fecentur', 'diffita' should read with s (euanescat, posito, statui, abscissae, respondebit, saltus, secentur, dissita).
In §36, the 'v' in 'Yv' and 'αvμ' is a lowercase italic v (the image shows ν in αν μ). This is fine.
